fatal.detail: The rewrite deleted the only qualifier that made C uniquely right, and option B is a mathematically valid decomposition of aggregate equity value, so the item is now double-keyed. In 'before' the stem pointed at one specific published decomposition ('The curriculum expresses the aggregate market value of equity, V_e, using three multiplicative components'), so 'which decomposition is it' had exactly one answer. The rewritten stem asks a free-standing factual question, 'The aggregate market value of equity in an economy is most likely expressed as the product of:', and under that stem B is true as written: aggregate book value x aggregate ROE = aggregate earnings, and aggregate earnings x aggregate P/E = aggregate market value of equity. That is an identity at any level of aggregation, not only at firm level. The after-rationale for B concedes the arithmetic ('Book value multiplied by return on equity gives earnings, and the P/E multiple capitalizes those earnings') and then rests the distinction entirely on a framing the stem no longer supplies ('It is not the aggregate market decomposition, which has to begin from the size of the economy rather than from a company's balance sheet') - a learner reading only the stem has no basis for preferring C. The citation did have to go under rule 9, but it needed replacing with a substantive restriction in the stem (e.g. asking for the decomposition that links aggregate equity value to the size of the economy), not simply dropping it.
fatal.quote_before: The curriculum expresses the aggregate market value of equity, V_e, using three multiplicative components. This decomposition is most likely: ... B: "V_e = Book value × Return on equity × P/E."
fatal.quote_after: The aggregate market value of equity in an economy is most likely expressed as the product of: ... B: "Book value, return on equity and the P/E multiple."

fatal.detail: The reframe cut the case anchor out of the stem and in doing so turned distractor B into a true statement. Before, the stem tied the question to one specific market ('In the Belvia case (Example 6), Dwight also faces high concentration risk in the equity market because most likely:'), so B was false as a matter of fact about that market — its rationale said only 'This is not the concentration described.' The rewritten stem asks a generic question, 'Concentration risk in a small emerging equity market most likely arises from:', and under that stem 'a single global technology company dominating the market' is a correct answer to it: one issuer dominating a market is concentration risk, and it is a more extreme concentration than the sector-plus-ownership mix in A. A and B now collide, with B defensible on the stem's own terms (a learner can point to Taiwan or Korea), so the item is no longer uniquely keyed to A. Nothing in the stem as rewritten lets the learner rule B out; only the vanished Belvia facts did that.
fatal.quote_before: STEM: "In the Belvia case (Example 6), Dwight also faces high concentration risk in the equity market because most likely:" / B: "The equity market is dominated by a single global technology company." / rationale B: "This is not the concentration described."
fatal.quote_after: STEM: "Concentration risk in a small emerging equity market most likely arises from:" / B: "a single global technology company dominating the market."

fatal.detail: Dropping the universal quantifier turned the B distractor into a defensible answer, so the item is now double-keyed against C. Before, B read 'Always overstate diversification benefits.' — false because of 'Always'. After, it reads 'overstate an asset's diversification value.', an unqualified statement under a stem that only asks what pairwise correlations 'are most likely to' do. The after-rationale for B concedes the direction does occur: 'Pairwise correlations can make a redundant asset appear diversifying', and defends B only with a qualifier that exists nowhere in the option text — 'they do not systematically overstate the benefit.' The sidebar example the key rests on (an asset that is an exact weighted combination of two holdings, adding no diversification value, yet showing only moderate pairwise correlations) is itself an overstatement of diversification value, so a learner reading B has a direct textual case for it. B is also now a strict subset of keyed C ('mismeasure an asset's diversification value.'): if B holds, C holds, so the two can no longer be separated without the rationale's unstated 'systematically'. Restoring 'always' (or 'systematically') to option B fixes it.

The stem is unchanged: "Alternative weighting schemes to market-cap weighting for the global market portfolio most likely include:". Distractor B's only falsifier was the word "only" — it was false because it asserted trailing-earnings weighting was the sole alternative, which is exactly what the old rationale said: "Earnings-weighting alone is not identified." With "only" deleted, B now claims merely that trailing-earnings weighting is among the alternatives to market-value weighting, which is defensible (it is the standard fundamental-indexation alternative), so the stem's "include" is satisfied. The rewritten rationale had to abandon the original reason and substitute a new, weaker one — "not among the alternatives identified. It is a fundamental-indexation idea rather than one of the recognized substitutes" — which concedes it is a weighting scheme. Key A ("GDP weighting or equal weighting") is still the curriculum-named answer but is now only arguably better than B rather than uniquely correct.

Same defect in the third option. "Book-value weighting only." was false because of "only", and the old rationale named that reason exactly: "Book value alone is not the identified alternative." Shortened to "Book-value weighting.", the option now asserts only that book-value weighting is one of the alternatives to market-cap weighting, which is true in the ordinary sense (book-value weighting is the canonical fundamental-index alternative). The new rationale, "Weighting by book value is likewise not the identified alternative. Like earnings weighting it is an accounting-based measure of size...", concedes it is a measure of size used for weighting, so it no longer establishes that the option is wrong. The item is left with three options that can each be read as true and only "most likely" separating key A from B and C.

The whole falsity of distractor A lived in its causal clause, and the rewrite deleted it. Before, A read "Capital preservation, because appraisal-based valuations give alternatives lower reported volatility than public equities." — false because it attributed capital preservation to appraisal smoothing. After, A is the bare role name "capital preservation." answering the stem "The roles that alternative investments play in a multi-asset portfolio most likely include:". Nothing now marks it wrong, and the item's own key rationale affirmatively endorses it: the after rationale for C lists among the roles "safe-haven characteristics in specific sub-strategies, such as some hedge fund strategies" — i.e. holding value in a drawdown, which is capital preservation. The after rationale for A tries to close this by asserting "so preservation of capital is not a role alternatives fill" (a sentence not present in before), so the item now contradicts itself: C's rationale says safe-haven/preservation is a role, A's rationale says it is not. A learner can defend A, so the item is ambiguous between A and C where before it was not.
fatal.quote_before: Capital preservation, because appraisal-based valuations give alternatives lower reported volatility than public equities.

fatal.detail: The reframed stem inverts the direction of the swap position. 'Pays a fixed rate of 2.8535% against a six-month MRR of 0.5925%' is the standard idiom for a PAY-fixed swap, and it contradicts the 'receive-fixed' label in the same clause; the before-stem avoided this by stating the rate without an operative verb ('receive-fixed swap at 2.8535%, 6m MRR 0.5925%'). Read literally, carry is -GBP1,130,500 and the 50 bp fall in rates produces a mark-to-market loss (the rationale's own approximation, 8.318 x GBP100M / 10,000 x 50 = GBP4,159,000, flips sign), so the six-month gain is about -GBP5,364,760. Among the three options the closest value is then A (GBP100,000), distance GBP5,464,760, against GBP10,729,520 for the keyed C -- the item is mis-keyed on its literal reading, not merely ambiguous. Rationale C still reasons from the receive-fixed side ('Swap carry is GBP1,130,500 = [(2.8535% - 0.5925%)/2] x GBP100 million' and 'the swap mark-to-market gain is GBP4,234,260'), so stem and rationale now describe opposite positions. All other inputs the reframe needed are present; the fix is the verb alone.
fatal.quote_before: In Example 3 (UK gilt vs GBP swap, 10-year, £100M notional, 50 bp rate fall over 6 months): 10y UK gilt at 2.25% coupon priced £93.947, YTM 2.9535%, vs 10y GBP receive-fixed swap at 2.8535%, 6m MRR 0.5925%, swap ModDur 8.318.
fatal.quote_after: a £100 million 10-year GBP receive-fixed swap pays a fixed rate of 2.8535% against a six-month MRR of 0.5925% and has a modified duration of 8.318

fatal.detail: Entry 577 (key A). The distractor lost the one word that made it false. Before, C was a definitional claim — the stem read "The reading's butterfly strategy for curvature is most likely:" and C answered "uses bullet-only exposure concentrated at a single maturity point"; "bullet-only" is what made it wrong, because a butterfly is never bullet-only. After, the stem reads "A yield curve butterfly strategy for curvature most likely involves:" and C reads "Bullet exposure concentrated at a single maturity." With "only" deleted and the stem's verb changed from "is" to "involves", C is now a true statement about a butterfly: the intermediate-term bullet body IS exposure concentrated at a single maturity, so a butterfly does involve it. Key A ("A long bullet paired with a short barbell, or the reverse") remains the fuller and better answer, but C is no longer wrong, and the rationale confirms the mismatch: after-rationale C still argues against the deleted qualifier — "A bullet concentrated at a single maturity is only the body of the trade. Without the offsetting barbell wings there is no exposure to curvature" — i.e. it rebuts a claim the option no longer makes (option C as it now reads does not exclude the wings). Fix is to restore the exclusivity, e.g. "Bullet exposure alone, concentrated at a single maturity."
fatal.quote_before: The butterfly strategy for curvature uses bullet-only exposure concentrated at a single maturity point.
fatal.quote_after: Bullet exposure concentrated at a single maturity.

fatal.detail: The rewrite replaced a three-word distractor rationale with invented arithmetic that is numerically false. Before, rationale C read in full: "Risk varies dramatically." After, it asserts that "the likelihood of credit loss at BB+ (940) is more than twice that at BBB- (610) and roughly eight times that at A- (180)." Neither ratio holds on the very factor table the item carries: 940/610 = 1.54, which is not more than twice, and 940/180 = 5.22, which is not roughly eight times. The figures themselves were preserved correctly from before (BBB- = 610, BB+ = 940, A- = 180, matching the before rationale's "BBB+=260, BBB=360, BBB-=610, BB+=940"), and the same after block gets the adjacent step right -- rationale A correctly says "The step from BBB- to BB+ alone is more than 300 factor points" (940 - 610 = 330). So this is one sentence the rewriter added on its own initiative, not content inherited from the source. Scope: key A is unaffected and the item is still answerable and single-keyed -- A ("default risk rises faster as ratings decline than ordinal spacing implies") remains the only true option against B ("all rating categories warrant identical treatment") and C ("credit risk does not differ across rating categories"). I am marking it fatal rather than style because the defect is a false quantitative claim shown to the learner after they commit, not prose that merely reads worse; the fix is to delete or correct the two ratios in rationale C.
fatal.quote_after: the likelihood of credit loss at BB+ (940) is more than twice that at BBB- (610) and roughly eight times that at A- (180)

fatal.detail: The rewrite deleted the limiting words that made C false. Before, C claimed personal discovery 'reduces to' age and gender — an exclusive claim, false against a stem that asks what discovery 'includes'. After, C is the bare noun phrase 'the client's age and gender', and the stem still reads 'most likely includes'. The client's age (and gender, for longevity and insurance purposes) genuinely is part of the personal information gathered, so C now reads as a true statement and collides with keyed B. C's own 'after' rationale also no longer describes the option as written: it argues against an exclusivity claim ('Age and gender barely begin the picture... a lifecycle rule keyed to two data points is not personal discovery') that the option no longer makes. The fix is to restore the limiter, e.g. 'the client's age and gender alone.'
fatal.quote_before: PERSONAL information reduces to the client's AGE and GENDER, the two data points that determine allocation under lifecycle models.

fatal.detail: Same deletion of the falsifying qualifier. Before, C asserted legal discovery 'is limited to confirming a WILL exists' and that trusts and powers of attorney are 'solely the estate attorney's concern' — false. After, C is simply 'confirmation that a will exists', under a stem that asks what the legal and estate information gathered 'most likely includes'. Confirming the existence of a will is unambiguously included in legal discovery, so C is now literally true and is no longer wrong for the reason its rationale gives. C's 'after' rationale is still written against the deleted claim ('Confirming that a will exists is the beginning of the inventory, not the whole of it'), i.e. it rebuts a 'limited to' statement the option no longer makes. Keyed B ('wills, trusts, and powers of attorney') is more complete, but the item now has two defensible answers. Restoring 'only'/'limited to' in C repairs it.
fatal.quote_before: LEGAL discovery is limited to confirming a WILL exists; trusts and powers of attorney are solely the estate attorney's concern.

fatal.detail: The item asks WHEN the policy was adopted, and after the rewrite nothing in the item supplies that date. Before, the timing fact lived in the option text and the stem named the case: stem 'QUINCO's ESG responsible investing policy has been in place most likely:' with keyed option A 'For the past seven years, based on three key considerations and objectives: acknowledgment that ESG factors along with traditional financial factors affect risk and return.' After, the option is stripped to a bare relative claim, 'Several years before the protest.', and the reframed stem supplies only the policy's three pillars ('built on ESG materiality to risk and return, transparency on material ESG issues, and long-term sustainability') plus the existence of a protest. It gives no horizon, no adoption date, no statement that the protest tested an existing policy or that the policy was only updated afterwards. A, B ('A few weeks before the protest.') and C ('Two years ago, in response to the protest.') are therefore all logically consistent with everything the item states; the choice turns entirely on the vignette fact 'in place for the past seven years', which the rewrite deleted along with the case name. The key's slot is still the true answer in the source case but is no longer derivable from the item, so the question is unanswerable as it now reads. (Checked: the seven-year fact appears nowhere in /home/user/CFA/CFAL3/Resources/reading_notes.json as curriculum content a learner could be expected to recall; it is case detail only.)
fatal.quote_before: QUINCO's ESG responsible investing policy has been in place most likely: / A: "For the past seven years, based on three key considerations and objectives: acknowledgment that ESG factors along with traditional financial factors affect risk and return."
fatal.quote_after: Students have protested an endowment's holding in a company facing child labor allegations. The endowment's ESG responsible investing policy, built on ESG materiality to risk and return, transparency on material ESG issues, and long-term sustainability, was most likely put in place: / A: "Several years before the protest."

fatal.detail: The reframe changed the question from "what does the sensitivity analysis show" to "which variable produces the largest reduction in IRR" — and under that new question A and C assert the SAME cause ("low traffic"), differing only in a number the stem never supplies. The stem gives the base case IRR (15%), the fixed-price contract, and the fact that low and high traffic cases were run; it gives no low-case IRR and no overrun IRR. So a learner can use the fixed-price-contract clue to eliminate B (cost risk is passed to the contractor), and is then left with two options that both answer the stem's question identically. Nothing in the item lets them prefer "10% to 11%" over "about 5%" — that discriminator exists only in the Year-0 dialogue the drill no longer reproduces, i.e. exactly the outside-the-item dependency rule 9 and the reframe ladder were meant to remove. In "before" the two options were at least distinguishable as whole statements of what the analysis showed, each carrying the base case plus its own case figure; the rewrite stripped A and C down to a shared stub plus an unsupported figure. The key is still factually right, but the item is no longer answerable from itself and C cannot be eliminated on reasoning. Fix is to put the low-case and overrun IRRs in the stem (ladder move 3) or to make the three options name three different causes (ladder move 2).
fatal.quote_before: stem: "Sensitivity analysis on the Sunnyland airport IRR most likely shows:" / A: "Base case 15% IRR; low-traffic case 10-11%." / C: "A base case of 15%; the low-traffic case pushes the IRR to roughly 5%, well below the project hurdle."
fatal.quote_after: stem: "...and the sponsor also runs reasonable low and high traffic cases. The largest reduction in the project's IRR most likely comes from:" / A: "low traffic, with an IRR of 10% to 11%." / C: "low traffic, with an IRR of about 5%."

fatal.detail: The rewrite deleted the item's only input and left nothing in its place, so the question is now unanswerable. In 'before', the only content distinguishing the three options was the figure pair carried by the key: options were 'A': 'Flat AUM.' / 'B': 'AUM decline.' / 'C': 'AUM growth from $50B to $56B.' In 'after' they are 'A': 'remained flat.' / 'B': 'declined.' / 'C': 'grew.' Flattening the figures-only-on-the-key shape was right, but the stem was only re-voiced, not reframed: 'Over the three years to R-SWF's interim review, its assets under management most likely:' supplies no starting AUM, no return, no flow and no market context, and R-SWF is a vignette entity the learner cannot open. Unlike the other R-SWF items in this slice (e.g. q12, q13, q14), where the distractors are implausible on reasoning alone, flat vs declined vs grew carries no internal asymmetry whatever, so the item is a blind one-in-three guess. The reframe ladder in the spec required move 1 (inline the data) or move 2 (ask the conceptual question); neither was taken. The inputs plainly existed: the 'after' C rationale still states 'Assets under management grew by $6 billion over the three years, from $50 billion to $56 billion.'
fatal.quote_after: stem: "Over the three years to R-SWF's interim review, its assets under management most likely:" with "C": "grew."

fatal.quote_before: R-SWF's ultimate ABC exit strategy (secondary sale) is most likely successful because:
fatal.quote_after: A sovereign wealth fund seeks to exit a 35% stake in a domestic beverage producer. The outcome is most likely:
fatal.detail: The reframe deleted the premise that made the item answerable and changed the question from cause to outcome. (1) Option C -- before 'No exit from ABC proved possible.', after 'No feasible exit from the stake.' -- was ruled out by the old stem's own words ('secondary sale ... successful'); the new stem asserts no outcome, so C is no longer excluded by anything in the item and the learner must recall how an unopenable case ended. (2) The stem supplies none of the inputs that identify the key: there is no weak local currency and no exporting buyer in it, so key B 'A sale to a strategic buyer with a hedging motive.' rests on facts that survive only inside rationale B ('whose sales had been adversely affected by a weaker local currency'). Held to the spec's reframe standard ('the reframed question must be answerable and unambiguous'), it fails: the item is now vignette recall. Remedy: restore the premise in the stem (an exit was achieved; the local currency had weakened and the buyer was an exporter into that market) and ask why the sale was available.

Double-keyed. The stem stopped naming the method under test, which turned distractor C into a second correct answer. BEFORE the stem fixed the method ('Composite return using beginning assets plus weighted cash flows most likely:') and C was false because it offered beginning-of-period-only weighting AS that method: 'R_C = Sigma [r_pi x (V_0,pi / Sigma V_0,pi)], using only beginning-of-period values with no adjustment for external cash flows.' AFTER, the stem only establishes that cash flows occurred and asks an open question about GIPS ('Under the GIPS standards, each portfolio's return is most likely weighted by its:'), and C reads 'beginning-of-period assets alone.' Asset-weighting by beginning-of-period values is itself one of the three GIPS-permitted methods and is not voided by the presence of external cash flows - the sibling item r15_gips_los_e_q1 (index 1142) states exactly that in its own 'after' rationale A: 'Composite returns must be calculated by asset-weighting the individual portfolio returns using beginning-of-period values, by a method that reflects both beginning-of-period values and external cash flows, or by the Aggregate Return method.' So key A ('beginning assets plus day-weighted external cash flows') and distractor C are now both correct answers to the stem as written, and C's rationale still rebuts the old stem rather than the new one, arguing only that C 'is the beginning-assets method' and that 'The beginning assets plus weighted cash flows method instead uses V_pi = V_0 + Sigma(CF_i x w_i)' - a method the rewritten stem never asks about. Fix by restoring the method name to the stem (e.g. 'Under the beginning assets plus weighted cash flows method, ...'), which makes C false again for its original reason.
fatal.quote_before: Composite return using beginning assets plus weighted cash flows most likely: ... C: "R_C = Sigma [r_pi x (V_0,pi / Sigma V_0,pi)], using only beginning-of-period values with no adjustment for external cash flows."
fatal.quote_after: A composite's constituent portfolios experienced external cash flows during the measurement period. Under the GIPS standards, each portfolio's return is most likely weighted by its: ... C: "beginning-of-period assets alone."

style.detail: Option A's assertion moved from a claim about the BASIS of universe design (index composition substituted for the firm's own process) to a claim about the universe's BREADTH (matching index breadth). The option is still false under the stem as rewritten -- the curriculum's criterion is the set of asset classes that receive a distinct allocation, kept otherwise as small as possible -- and rationale A in "after" still argues the original point ("Letting index composition set the universe ignores the firm's own investment process"), so the item is not broken and the key at C is unaffected. But the detail that carried the falsity explicitly ("without regard to firm-specific portfolio needs") is gone, leaving a distractor whose wrongness the learner must infer from the "as small as possible" guidance rather than read off the option. Worth noting as the one place in entries 0-9 where a distractor's claim is not the same claim said tersely. Not fatal: no collision with B ("as large as possible") or C, and A remains clearly wrong.
style.quote_before: Based on capitalization-weighted major indices without regard to firm-specific portfolio needs.
style.quote_after: as broad as the major capitalization-weighted indices.

style.detail: Distractor C gained a claim it did not previously make. Before, C asserted one direction (risk overestimated) plus a causal clause; the rewrite deleted the clause (correct under rule 1) but added a second, new assertion about expected return, turning C into the exact mirror of A. Not fatal: C is still false, still false for the same underlying reason, and rationale C in 'after' does cover both halves ('Both directions run the other way ... makes the sample overstate rather than understate ex ante expected return'). But per the per-letter same-claim requirement this is drift, not compression — the learner is now being asked to reject a proposition the item never put to them before.
style.quote_before: Overestimate ex ante risk because currency risk was still priced into asset yields.
style.quote_after: Overestimate ex ante risk and underestimate expected return.

style.detail: The key's own option lost the qualifier that located it. 'Cyclical' was the word that marked consumer confidence as a business-cycle phenomenon rather than a trend shock, and that is precisely the distinction the rewritten stem now turns on ('exogenous shocks to a country's trend rate of economic growth'). The 'after' rationale still reasons from the deleted word — 'A swing in consumer confidence is a business cycle phenomenon — a fluctuation around the trend' — so the rationale argues a qualifier the option no longer carries. Not fatal: consumer confidence appears on none of the six named shock categories (policy changes, new products and technologies, geopolitics, natural disasters, natural resources and critical inputs, financial crises) with or without 'cyclical', so A remains the unique correct answer and B and C remain on the list.
style.quote_before: A cyclical decline in consumer confidence.
style.quote_after: Weaker consumer confidence.

style.detail: Two linked residues. (1) Option A dropped 'then publishing the result', but rationale A still rests part of its argument on publishing — 'publishing on that basis passes the data-mining bias on to the reader' — so the rationale describes a clause the option no longer reads. (2) The compression moved A toward B: A is now 'Construct an economic explanation', B is 'Require an explicit economic rationale', and the only things separating them are A's 'once found' and B's out-of-sample test, where the 'before' pair were separated by the much blunter 'Inventing a plausible story ... after the fact'. Checked for collision and it does not collide: the stem asks for the 'most appropriate safeguard', and B alone carries the out-of-sample test, so B is still clearly best. Worth tightening A rather than fixing the key.
style.quote_before: Inventing a plausible story to explain the finding after the fact, then publishing the result.
style.quote_after: Construct an economic explanation for the relationship once found.

style.detail: The rewrite added explicit arithmetic to rationale A that does not match the figure option A actually carries. Option A is 4.0% (unchanged), but the new rationale works the subtraction out loud as 0.7% + 1.5% + 2.0% = 4.2%, hedged only by the word 'roughly'. The 'before' rationale made the same latent claim ('This value omits the dividend yield contribution') without exposing the 0.2pp gap, so nothing substantive changed; the rewrite just put a number on the page that contradicts the option it is explaining. Key C (6.0% = 0.7 + 1.5 + 2.0 + 1.8) is exact and still uniquely correct, so the item is not broken - the rationale simply now reads as if it describes an option that says 4.2%.
style.quote_before: A: "This value omits the dividend yield contribution."
style.quote_after: A: "This is roughly the nominal trend growth figure on its own — labor input growth plus labor productivity growth plus inflation, 0.7% + 1.5% + 2.0% = 4.2% — with the 1.8% dividend yield omitted." (option A reads "4.0%.")

style.detail: Reframed although the 'before' item was already self-contained, which the spec forbids ('Do not reframe an item that is already self-contained' — the old stem cited no exhibit and no curriculum text, so only rules 1-8 applied). The reframe is not wrong — key C is still the only correct direction and A/B are still false — but the correct option's second clause, which is the part of the LOS the item was testing, is now absent from the option set, leaving a bare sign question. The 'shorter-term yields rise more but with less price impact' nuance survives only in rationale C, i.e. after the learner has committed. A restatement under rules 1-8 would have shortened option C to something like 'Capital losses, concentrated in longer maturities.' and kept the tested distinction in play.
style.quote_before: stem: "Rising expected inflation that stays within the cyclical range would most likely affect nominal bonds by:" / C: "Generating capital losses as the expected-inflation component of yields rises; shorter-term yields rise more but with less price impact than longer yields."
style.quote_after: stem: "Rising expected inflation that stays within the expected cyclical range would most likely cause nominal bond prices to:" / A: "rise." B: "remain unchanged." C: "fall."

style.detail: Same pattern: reframed from a claim-selection item to a direction item although the 'before' stem was already self-contained, so the reframe ladder was not available to it. Substance is intact — key B 'rise.' is correct, A and C are still false, and rationale B keeps the idiosyncrasy caveat about lease length and the supply pipeline — but the reframe was triggered by option length (option C carried generator junk, 'That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay'), which a straight rewrite under rules 1-2 would have cured without changing what the item asks. Note also that rationale A still opens by rebutting a premise the option no longer states.
style.quote_before: stem: "Higher-than-expected inflation is most likely to affect real estate as follows:" / A: "Real estate is neutral because leases lock in nominal rates permanently." B: "Real estate benefits, coinciding with high demand, expectations of rental income rising faster than general inflation, and rising property values."
style.quote_after: stem: "Higher-than-expected inflation is most likely to cause property values and expected rental income to:" / A: "remain flat." B: "rise." C: "decline." / rationale A: "Leases do not lock in nominal rates permanently."

style.quote_before: No meaningful relationship with corporate excess returns.
style.quote_after: No meaningful change in excess returns on investment-grade corporate bonds.
style.detail: The distractor's claim shifts from 'no relationship' (a statement about correlation, which is what the item tests) to 'no meaningful change' (a statement about the level of excess returns). Its own rationale in 'after' still rebuts the old wording -- 'The relationship is meaningful and positive, with correlations of about 0.28 at a one-quarter horizon and 0.39 at a one-year horizon' -- so the rationale describes the option as it read before, not as it now reads. Not fatal: the option remains false either way and B is still the unambiguous best answer.

style.quote_before: Central banks explicitly coordinate real rate targeting internationally.
style.quote_after: Central banks coordinate real rate targets internationally.
style.detail: The qualifier 'explicitly' was dropped, and that qualifier is the hinge the rationale still turns on: 'Co-movement does not depend on explicit international coordination of real rate targets.' The option now makes the broader (and looser) claim that central banks coordinate real rate targets at all. Not fatal -- central banks do not target real rates, let alone coordinate such targets, so the option is still clearly wrong and the rationale's second clause ('not from any coordination agreement') still covers it -- but the distractor lost the word that made it crisply false.

All three rationales in 'after' refute or support their option by appeal to a specific market the rewritten stem no longer identifies, so they no longer describe the options as the learner now reads them. The key's rationale opens 'In the market at issue roughly half of the public equity market capitalization is represented by companies in the natural resources sector'; B is dismissed as 'not the concentration described in this market'; C is dismissed with 'The market contains substantial large companies'. With the Belvia setup gone from the stem, 'the market at issue' and 'this market' point at nothing the learner has seen, and the refutation of B reduces to an assertion about hidden facts rather than a reason. This is the same gap that makes the fatal finding above bite; even if B were reworded, the rationales would need to argue from the generic stem rather than from an unnamed market.
style.quote_before: rationale A: "Correct. The reading states roughly half of the public equity market is represented by natural resource companies..." / rationale B: "This is not the concentration described." / rationale C: "The reading does not describe this concentration."
style.quote_after: rationale A: "In the market at issue roughly half of the public equity market capitalization is represented by companies in the natural resources sector" / rationale B: "not the concentration described in this market" / rationale C: "The market contains substantial large companies, including the natural resource producers"

style.detail: Rationale B invents a substantive defence of the distractor that was not in 'before' and that sits awkwardly against the reading itself. The option is 'requires normality, and cannot handle time variation'; it is false because of the normality half, and 'before' said only that the pair is not the one identified. The rewrite instead tells the learner that a constant sample matrix 'handles time variation no worse than the alternatives it is being compared with'. That is defensible only within this question's comparison set (multi-factor and shrinkage matrices are also constant); read on its own it contradicts the reason the same reading goes on to introduce ARCH, namely that volatility is time-varying and a constant matrix cannot capture it. Not fatal: option B is still wrong, the key still sits on A, and the rationale does end with 'Neither item is one of the two problems identified.' Recommend trimming the clause to the non-identification point.
style.quote_before: Neither of these is the specific pair identified.
style.quote_after: a constant sample matrix handles time variation no worse than the alternatives it is being compared with

style.detail: The keyed option now refers to 'the two coefficients' but the stem no longer names or defines them. 'Before' at least pointed at the standard ARCH notation on the face of the options ('The parameter beta = 0', '(alpha + beta)'); the rewrite replaced those with 'A shock coefficient of zero' and 'A high sum of the two coefficients' while the stem was shortened to a single clause that introduces no model and no parameters, so the phrase has no antecedent in the item. A drill shows one question at a time, so the learner cannot pick the antecedent up from the neighbouring ARCH item (index 127), which does describe the specification. Not fatal, because within an ARCH model the two coefficients (on lagged variance and on the squared shock) are unambiguous and B is the only one of the three that could explain clustering at all. Fix is one clause in the stem, e.g. naming the coefficients on the lagged variance and the squared shock.
style.quote_before: According to the reading, the reason volatility 'clusters' at high or low levels in an ARCH model is most likely that: ... B. The higher the parameter (α + β), the more the variance 'remembers' what happened in the past.
style.quote_after: In an ARCH model, the clustering of volatility at high or low levels is most likely explained by: ... B. A high sum of the two coefficients.

style.detail: The rewritten C rationale still rebuts a clause that was deleted from option C. In "before", option C read "A rise in required return, so an overweight allocation is not warranted." — the overweight claim was part of the option. In "after", option C is only "A rise in the required return.", but its rationale closes by contrasting "attractive instead of unwarranted", which now answers a claim the learner never saw. style.quote_before: C option: "A rise in required return, so an overweight allocation is not warranted."
style.quote_after: C option: "A rise in the required return." / C rationale: "the resulting price adjustment is what makes an overweight allocation attractive instead of unwarranted."

Before, each element was explicitly a PV; after, two of the three are named as flows ("pension income", "expected inheritances"), which on an extended economic balance sheet are assets only as present values. The claim is not changed in substance and A remains unambiguously the best of the three (B and C are plainly conventional financial assets), and the rationale restores the PV wording in full ("the present value of expected pension income; and the present value of expected inheritances"), so this is imprecision rather than a broken question. Not fatal; noted because the stem asks what extended portfolio *assets* include.

style.detail: The reframed stem drops the qualifier 'beyond volatility', which was what made the keyed option an exact answer and what set up the contrast with distractor C. The new stem asks for the full set of risk measures a mean-variance allocation can incorporate, but option B ('tracking risk and downside risk measures.') omits volatility itself -- which the item's own after-rationale for C concedes is incorporated ('Volatility is the baseline risk measure of the approach, not the only one it can accommodate.'). Not fatal: B carries no 'only' while A ('only tail risk measures...') and C ('volatility only.') are both exclusive and both false, so B is still unambiguously best and the key has not moved. Restoring 'beyond volatility' (or 'in addition to volatility') to the stem would make B exact again.
style.quote_before: A mean–variance asset allocation most likely can incorporate risk sensitivities beyond volatility, including:
style.quote_after: The risk measures that a mean-variance asset allocation can incorporate are most likely:

style.detail: Distractor C lost the universal qualifier "always". Before it read as an absolute claim that was false on its face; after, it is a general claim that is closer to defensible, since thin history genuinely is a problem for some narrow segments. Not fatal: the item is still single-keyed on B against the "most likely problematic because" stem, the exclusion in "before" did not rest on "always" either (its rationale said data availability is a secondary concern, not the primary reason), and the "after" rationale re-establishes the falsity by noting that many sub-asset classes do have long series available and that thin history is a secondary concern rather than the central objection. Flagged because qualifier deletion on a distractor is exactly the pattern this pass risks, and a reviewer should confirm the blanket claim is still read as false. Compare the sibling item r3_oaa_los_e_q7, where the same deletion (option C losing "only") was compensated by changing the stem verb from "include" to "comprises"; no such compensation was made here.
style.quote_before: Sub-asset classes always have insufficient historical data for optimization.
style.quote_after: sub-asset classes lack sufficient history for optimization.

style.detail: The keyed option lost the hedge that made it literally accurate. Before: 'Equity risk can be the dominant risk exposure even in a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.' After: 'Equity risk dominates a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.' The after-rationale still carries the hedged form — 'equity risk can be the dominant risk exposure even in a seemingly well-diversified portfolio' — so the option and its own rationale no longer say the same thing: the option asserts that equity risk does dominate such a portfolio, which is not a claim the reading makes. B remains clearly the best of the three (A is a separate implementation issue, C is explicitly denied) and the item is still answerable and correctly keyed, so this is not fatal, but 'can dominate' should be restored.
style.quote_before: Equity risk can be the dominant risk exposure even in a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.
style.quote_after: Equity risk dominates a seemingly well-diversified portfolio.

style.quote_before: W* = (μ − rf) × σ.
style.quote_after: Varies with excess return per unit of volatility, independent of risk aversion.
style.detail: The reframe reversed the direction of B's error in volatility. Before, B was wrong partly because it MULTIPLIED the risk premium by volatility: option "W* = (μ − rf) × σ." As rewritten, "per unit of volatility" states the opposite operation — the risk premium DIVIDED by σ (a Sharpe-ratio-like quantity). The option's own rationale was not updated to match and still asserts the old multiplication: "This formulation leaves risk aversion out altogether and mishandles variance, scaling by volatility instead, as in w* = (μ − rf) × σ." So the rationale describes a formula the option no longer states, violating the spec's requirement that a distractor's rationale "still has to describe it." Not keyed-breaking: B remains false on the surviving "independent of risk aversion" clause, and key C ("Falls with risk aversion and rises with excess return per unit of variance") is still the unambiguous best answer against A ("Rises with both risk aversion and variance"), whose rationale does match its option. Fix is to re-voice B as scaling with volatility (e.g. "Varies with excess return times volatility, independent of risk aversion") or to correct the rationale's formula.

The key's option now asserts something the stem has just removed from the problem. The stem reads "For an unconstrained mean-variance optimization, in which no budget constraint forces the weights to sum to 1" - so there is no budget constraint for the weights to breach, and option C has the mirror-image problem ("satisfy the budget constraint"). The after-rationale concedes the contradiction in as many words: "the solution does not respect a budget constraint that was never imposed." The substantive claim is unchanged and A is still uniquely correct (B is a frontier, not a point; C is the constrained outcome), so the item is not broken - but "that fail to sum to 100%" would carry the same claim without arguing against the stem. The dropped reverse-optimization qualifier is adequately covered by the stem's "most likely" and survives in the rationale.
style.quote_before: A single set of weights that is typically relatively extreme, with very large long and short positions, and which will not sum to 100% except in special reverse-optimization cases.
style.quote_after: Extreme long and short weights that breach the budget constraint.

style.detail: The expansion of distractor A's rationale added a clause whose sense is inverted. The before text was just "lambda = 0.5 corresponds to an aggressive investor with low risk aversion." The after text appends that such an investor "would accept a large variance penalty in exchange for expected return" - but the variance penalty in U = E(R) - 0.005(lambda)(sigma squared) is proportional to lambda, so at lambda = 0.5 the penalty the investor applies is small, not large. What the aggressive investor accepts is large variance, not a large penalty; as written it describes high risk aversion. Compare the correctly worded parallel clause in the after-rationale for C, "penalizing variance so heavily that the investor would hold a near-riskless allocation." The option itself (0.5) and the key (4) are unaffected, so this reads worse rather than breaking the item.
style.quote_before: λ = 0.5 corresponds to an aggressive investor with low risk aversion.
style.quote_after: A λ of 0.5 sits below the 1–10 range into which most investors' risk aversion falls and corresponds to an aggressive investor with low risk aversion, who would accept a large variance penalty in exchange for expected return.

style.detail: The rewritten stem stacks two CFA qualifiers on top of each other: "the most appropriate remedy is most likely:". The spec (rule 8) wants the stem to end with one qualifier, and the bank's own examples carry exactly one ("is closest to", "is most likely"). The original carried the qualifier once ("the reading recommends most likely"). Substance is unaffected -- key B ("Using the Black-Litterman model") is still the only approach that keeps the equilibrium anchor while admitting views, A and C both remain wrong for the reasons their rationales still give -- so this reads worse rather than breaking anything. Fix is to drop one: "the most appropriate remedy is to:" or "the recommended remedy is most likely:".
style.quote_before: For those with minor objections to using market-cap weights alone, the reading recommends most likely:
style.quote_after: the most appropriate remedy is most likely:

style.detail: The item was reframed off Exhibit 9 and the stem now reads generically ('A Monte Carlo projection of a retiree's wealth'), with no currency, no investor and no figures. The key's rationale still quotes the exhibit's CAF$ amounts, so a currency code that the self-contained stem never introduces appears from nowhere in the explanation. Not a defect in the question: option B is correct, A and C are false, every letter carries its prior claim, and the stem is answerable from itself. The fix would be to say 'a few hundred thousand' and 'ten times that' or to introduce the currency in the stem.

style.detail: The rewrite made the keyed option the conspicuously longest of the three, where before the longest option was a distractor, so the "take the longest option" heuristic now names the key. After: A = 58 chars, B (key) = 88 chars, C = 64 chars. Before: A = 70, B = 122, C = 145, so length did not point at B. This is the length-asymmetry leak the spec calls a working answer key (drill_house_style.md lines 29-31, 41-42). Not fatal: each letter carries the same claim it carried before, B is still the only correct definition of minimum expectations, and both distractors remain false per their own rationales. B could carry the identical claim in distractor-length form, e.g. "The minimum return expected over the horizon at a given probability of success."
style.quote_before: B. "The minimum return expected to be earned over the given time horizon with a given minimum required probability of success." (122 chars) against distractor C. "The arithmetic mean of expected returns across the goal's investment horizon. The plain expected return carries no success-probability qualifier." (145 chars)
style.quote_after: B. "The minimum return expected over the horizon at a given required probability of success." (88 chars) against A. "The lowest return observed historically for the asset mix." (58) and C. "The arithmetic mean of expected returns over the goal's horizon." (64)

style.detail: Rationale A names a different second interpretation than the keyed option C does, so the two rationales disagree about what the pair is. Rationale A (after): 'The rebalancing story is instead the diversification return and the return to supplying liquidity - buying the asset class that has weakened and selling the one that has strengthened.' Rationale C (after) and option C instead give 'A diversification return and a short volatility return.' A learner who reads A first is told the second interpretation is liquidity supply, then told by C it is short volatility. IMPORTANT CAVEAT: this is NOT introduced by the rewrite - the identical sentence is already in before's rationale A ('Momentum and value are EQUITY factor premia; the rebalancing interpretations are the diversification return and being a supplier of liquidity (buying weakness, selling strength).'), and before's option A leaked the same text into the option itself. The rewrite only removed the leak from the option, which is an improvement. The key sits correctly in C, option C makes the same claim it made before, and A and B remain false. I report it only so the defect is on record; no rewrite action is implicated, and the item is otherwise sound.
style.quote_before: Incorrect. Momentum and value are EQUITY factor premia; the rebalancing interpretations are the diversification return and being a supplier of liquidity (buying weakness, selling strength).
style.quote_after: The rebalancing story is instead the diversification return and the return to supplying liquidity — buying the asset class that has weakened and selling the one that has strengthened.

style.detail: Distractor A lost the exclusivity qualifier that made it false. Before, A claimed regulatory position limits were THE MAIN disadvantage of growing AUM — an over-claim, false on its face regardless of whether position limits bite at all. After, the stem reads 'As assets under management grow, investment managers most likely incur disadvantages including:' and A is merely one item in a non-exclusive list, so the option now asserts only that narrower opportunity sets from regulatory position limits are AMONG the disadvantages of scale. That is defensible in substance (large managers do run into ownership/position limits that shrink the investable set), so the option is no longer cleanly false; its falsity now rests entirely on the curriculum's list of three being closed, which the item does not say. The key is not displaced — C still reproduces the curriculum's three disadvantages verbatim (larger trade sizes/price impact, style drift from inflows, slower decision making) and remains clearly the best of the three — so the item is not double-keyed, but the distractor is weaker than it was and the rationale ('not among the disadvantages of manager scale identified here') now has to appeal to an unstated closed list rather than to anything wrong in the option itself.
style.quote_before: The main AUM disadvantage is a narrower opportunity set imposed by regulatory position limits. That specification would be used as-is, with no forward-looking overlay. Applied uniformly, it would bind at every horizon and every asset class.
style.quote_after: narrower opportunity sets imposed by regulatory position limits.

style.detail: Distractor A's attributed mechanism changed subject. Before, the false claim was about dealer behavior causing total market failure ("Dealers withdrew market-making capital across fixed-income markets, so even government bonds became impossible to sell."); after, it is about asset owners' own inability to sell ("owners could not sell even their government bonds."). The dealer/market-making clause is gone entirely. This is NOT fatal: the falsifying core (government bonds were unsellable) survives, so A is still wrong for the same reason, the "after" rationale still describes it ("The most liquid assets, such as government bonds, remained saleable throughout"), key B ("owners sold their most liquid assets first, raising the illiquid share.") is still the single correct answer, and C is still the reversed mechanism. Flagged only so the claim-identity drift in this letter is on record; no edit is required for the item to work.
style.quote_before: Dealers withdrew market-making capital across fixed-income markets, so even government bonds became impossible to sell.
style.quote_after: owners could not sell even their government bonds.

style.detail: The rewrite added a fabricated, self-contradicting derivation to distractor A's rationale. It asserts the 25.0% answer "comes from applying the tax rate as a direct multiple rather than through the (1 - t) relationship" and then names that supposed error as "0.10 / 0.40". 0.40 is neither the tax rate (0.25) nor (1 - t) (0.75), so the denominator it attributes to the mistaken candidate has no relation to the tax rate at all, and the two halves of the sentence describe different errors. The arithmetic is incidentally true (0.10/0.40 = 0.25), and the rationale still tells the learner the correct conversion, so the item remains correctly keyed and answerable; the invented error path merely reads worse than the original one-liner it replaced. The real trap is simply mistaking the tax rate for the range.
style.quote_before: This is far too wide.
style.quote_after: This is far too wide. It comes from applying the tax rate as a direct multiple rather than through the (1 - t) relationship: the correct conversion is R_at = R_pt / (1 - t) = 0.10 / 0.75 = 13.3%, not 0.10 / 0.40 or any similar form that produces 25%. The equivalent range widens only modestly at a 25% tax rate.

style.detail: Option A no longer states a claim about trend signals; it names a thing that is not a candidate trend signal at all. Before, A asserted a proposition the learner could judge true or false ("Trend signals assume asset prices follow a random walk with no exploitable direction."). After, A is a noun phrase, "A random walk in prices over the trailing 12 months", offered as an answer to "A basic trend signal used in systematic TAA is most likely:" — a random walk is a price process, not a signal, so the option is a category error rather than a wrong signal. It also breaks the parallelism of rule 7: B and C are both return measures ("The most recent 12-month return." / "The average return over the past 30 years.") while A is a process description, which makes A visibly the odd one out and narrows the real choice to B versus C. Not fatal: A is still unambiguously not the answer, the key B is still correct and clearly best, and rationale A still explains the same reason it is wrong ("If asset prices followed a random walk, past returns would carry no information about future returns and trend following would be pointless."). The repair is to keep A a signal, e.g. "A randomly selected direction for the next 12 months."
style.quote_before: Trend signals assume asset prices follow a random walk with no exploitable direction.
style.quote_after: A random walk in prices over the trailing 12 months.

style.detail: Rationale C's statement of the purpose of ESG integration was tightened from a disjunction to a conjunction, which overstates the curriculum claim: the goals are to reduce risk and/or enhance returns, not necessarily both. The keyed answer (C, ESG integration) is unaffected and the item remains correctly single-keyed; this is a fidelity slip inside the rationale text only.
style.quote_before: The goals of ESG integration are to reduce financial risks and/or enhance financial returns by identifying and valuing risks or opportunities that are not typically identified and valued.
style.quote_after: The goals of ESG integration are to reduce financial risks and enhance financial returns by identifying and valuing risks or opportunities that are not typically identified and valued.

style.detail: Rationale B now opens with a sentence that inverts the concept it is explaining. Before, the rationale correctly located the disadvantage in the instability of the categories; after, the first clause literally asserts that stability itself is the disadvantage, and only the clause after the colon ('the categories may change over time') restores the actual reasoning. A learner reading the first clause alone is told the opposite of the curriculum point. The key does not move and the enumerated four advantages are preserved in full, so this is wording, not a broken question.
style.quote_before: Correct. The reading explicitly identifies as a *disadvantage* that size/style categories may change over time and may be defined differently among investors.
style.quote_after: Stability is a disadvantage of size/style segmentation, not an advantage: the categories may change over time, and they may be defined differently among investors.

style.detail: The keyed option dropped the absolute qualifier 'Perfect'. Flagging it because qualifier loss on a keyed option is the pattern this audit hunts, but I judge it non-fatal: the curriculum lists as a disadvantage that size/style categories may change over time and may be defined differently among investors, and advantage (4) is specifically accommodation of a company's changing growth/value orientation, so plain 'Stability of size/style classifications over time' is still not one of the four advantages. B remains the clear answer and A and C remain genuine advantages, so the item is not double-keyed or arguable; the rewrite merely removed a redundant giveaway.
style.quote_before: Perfect stability of size/style classification over time.
style.quote_after: Stability of size/style classifications over time.

style.detail: The rewrite promoted the stem from identifying one hidden cost to ranking it as the largest. Before: "The reading identifies a hidden cost faced by index funds — most likely:". After: "For an index fund, the most significant hidden cost is most likely:". The source material supports only existence, not primacy — rationale C in "after" still says "Index funds face a hidden cost from potential predatory trading" and never claims it is the most significant, so the rationale no longer supports the stem it now sits under. Not fatal: A ("a commission premium over active managers") is false and B ("none, given low turnover and transparency") is false, so the key in slot C remains correct and clearly the best of the three. The fix is to drop "most significant" (e.g. "For an index fund, a hidden cost of trading is most likely:").

style.detail: Distractor A lost the absolute qualifier that carried its falsity. Before it claimed results were "fully explained by factor exposures" (an overreach the rationale rebuts); after it claims only that results are "explained by factor exposures", which is a defensible reading of the empirical literature. The option is still wrong against the stem because "successful before fees" is not what the reading says, and keyed C ("unsuccessful at beating benchmarks while charging high fees") remains clearly best, so this is not fatal — but the softened claim is weaker than the one the "after" rationale for A argues against ("the record is not described as gross outperformance that is subsequently explained away by exposures to size, value, or momentum").

style.quote_after: successful before fees, with results explained by factor exposures.

style.detail: The stem dropped the belief hedge and now asserts as fact what the reading (and the item's own keyed rationale) presents as an investor belief. Before, the stem asked why "investors often believe potential alpha is most likely reduced"; after, it asserts that "the potential for alpha is most likely reduced". The B rationale in "after" still reads "investors often believe that potential alpha is substantially reduced because all publicly available information is efficiently disseminated, analyzed, and reflected in stock prices", so the stem now states more than the rationale supports. Key B is unaffected and both distractors remain false, so the item is still answerable and correctly keyed.
style.quote_before: The reading notes that in large-cap developed markets investors often believe potential alpha is most likely reduced because:
style.quote_after: In large-cap developed markets, the potential for alpha is most likely reduced because:

style.detail: Option B was a standalone proposition; compressed into the new stem frame it reads as self-contradiction. Before, the stem was "The reading identifies two examples of non-investable indexes. These are most likely:" with B as a full sentence. After, the stem is "Non-investable equity indexes most likely include:" and B is the lowercase continuation "no equity indexes.", so the item now reads "Non-investable equity indexes most likely include no equity indexes." The underlying claim (that no equity index is non-investable) survives and the rationale still rebuts exactly that claim, so the key is unaffected and it is not fatal — but the option no longer states its claim cleanly, and B is also the only one of the three that is not a named index or set of indexes, breaking the parallelism rule 7 asks for.
style.quote_before: No equity index is non-investable.
style.quote_after: no equity indexes.

style.detail: De-citing the stem swapped a curriculum attribution for an empirical size ranking the curriculum does not make. "The reading identifies five major equity index providers" is a claim about what the reading names; "The five largest global equity index providers are..." asserts a global ranking. That assertion is shaky on its own terms (CRSP and Morningstar are not plausibly among the five largest index providers by revenue or by assets tracked, whereas Nasdaq — distractor C — arguably is), so the rewrite slightly strengthens the distractor it is meant to exclude. Not fatal: the item still asks only which firm completes the stated list, S&P Dow Jones is the curriculum's fifth and is unambiguously a top index provider, and Nasdaq is still not on the list of five, so B remains clearly best. The fix is to drop the superlative — "Major global equity index providers include CRSP, FTSE Russell, Morningstar, MSCI, and most likely:" — which meets rule 9 without asserting a ranking.

style.quote_after: The five largest global equity index providers are CRSP, FTSE Russell, Morningstar, MSCI, and most likely:

style.detail: The rationale for distractor C keeps its original reason (Nasdaq is an exchange operator, not one of the five named providers) but appends a sentence with no counterpart in "before" and no bearing on why C is wrong. Naming Nasdaq as the fifth provider does not "understate how many firms publish rule-based, investable benchmarks" — the count of benchmark publishers is not what the option gets wrong, and the sentence invites the learner to reason that there are in fact more than five providers, which cuts against the stem. Rationale padding only; the first sentence already does the work. Everything else in this item's rationales is faithfully carried over.
style.quote_before: Nasdaq operates the Nasdaq family of indexes but is not among the five broad providers the reading names.
style.quote_after: Naming Nasdaq as the remaining provider also understates how many firms publish rule-based, investable benchmarks that tracking portfolios are built against.

style.detail: Distractor B gained a clause it did not carry before. Before, B asserted only the inverse convexity-duration relationship; after, it leads with the TRUE proposition that duration rises linearly with maturity and only its second clause is false. The option is still wrong (a conjunction with one false clause), it is still wrong for the same reason, and rationale B still describes it correctly ('The relationship is direct, not inverse'), so the item is NOT broken and the key at A is still uniquely best. Flagging only because the per-letter claim text genuinely changed: the addition appears to be a parallelism move so that all three options share the same two-clause shape. No action needed unless the audit wants distractor claims held byte-for-byte.
style.quote_before: For zeros, convexity is inversely proportional to duration, so longer-duration zeros carry systematically less convexity.
style.quote_after: duration rises linearly with maturity and convexity falls as duration rises.

style.detail: Key A and distractor B now differ only by the words "compounded" and "multiplied", and under one natural reading they say the same thing. Before, B carried its own arithmetic and was unambiguously false: it asserted the bare product of the two NET returns, R_DC = R_FC x R_FX, which is visibly not (1 + R_FC)(1 + R_FX) - 1. The rewrite stripped that formula, leaving "the foreign-currency and currency returns multiplied" -- but compounding IS the multiplication of the two GROSS returns, so a learner who reads B as "multiply the returns (as 1 + R factors)" sees a second correct option. A is still the better answer, because "compounded" is the curriculum's own word for the relationship and the stem asks for the most likely, so this is not mis-keyed or double-keyed; but the distractor lost the detail that made it cleanly wrong, and the option set no longer stands on its own -- only B's rationale ("The bare product R_FC x R_FX is only the cross-term of that expansion") restores the distinction, and the learner reads that after committing. The fix is to keep the distinction visible in the option itself, e.g. "The foreign-currency and currency returns multiplied together as a cross-product."
style.quote_before: The domestic-currency return on a foreign bond is the product of the two returns: R_DC = R_FC × R_FX.
style.quote_after: The foreign-currency and currency returns multiplied.

style.detail: The reframed stem predicates "is least likely" directly on three gerund phrases, so the item reads "a recommended practice is least likely: Maximizing turnover to increase active management alpha." The before-stem asked "Which of the following is least likely one of them?", which governed the imperative options cleanly; the new stem needs "is least likely to be:" (or "the practice least likely to be recommended is:") to govern gerunds. Substance is untouched: all five key points are preserved in rationale C, C is still the only non-recommended practice, and A and B are both still genuine key points with rationales that describe them as they now read. Style only, not broken.
style.quote_before: The reading identifies five key points for managing taxable FI portfolios. Which of the following is least likely one of them?
style.quote_after: In managing a taxable fixed-income portfolio, a recommended practice is least likely:

style.detail: The keyed option's content was broadened rather than restated tersely: before, B named two liability-based approaches (cash flow matching and duration matching, each with its definition in parentheses); after, it names three (cash flow matching, duration matching, and contingent immunization). This is a genuine change to what letter B asserts, not a shortening of the same assertion. It is not fatal: the stem asks what liability-based mandates 'most likely include', the before-rationale for B already enumerated all three approaches as the liability-based family, so the new B is still true, still the best of the three, and the key has not moved. A ('Cash flow matching and contingent immunization, but not duration matching') remains false because duration matching is liability-based, and C ('Duration matching, understood as matching each liability payout with a bond cash flow') remains false because that describes cash flow matching, so no collision or double key is created. Flagged only because the spec's 'the correct option makes the same claim it made before, said tersely' was not what happened here.
style.quote_before: Cash flow matching (attempts to ensure all future liability payouts are matched precisely by cash flows from bonds or fixed-income derivatives) and duration matching (based on the duration of assets and liabilities, so both are similarly affected by interest rate changes).
style.quote_after: Cash flow matching, duration matching, and contingent immunization.

style.detail: The key's slot no longer carries the claim it carried. Before, B was a decision-process statement: "The decision to build a laddered bond portfolio should be weighed against buying shares in a fixed-income mutual fund, especially if the portfolio consists of a limited number of corporate bonds." After, it is a substantive comparative claim: "it diversifies default risk less well than a fixed-income mutual fund." That is one of the three reasons the curriculum gives for weighing the decision (the others, greater cost of acquisition and slower/worse liquidation, are still in the rationale but no longer in the option), so the option is a narrowing to a subset rather than a terse restatement. It remains true, remains supported by the after rationale ("The mutual fund clearly provides greater diversification of default risk"), and remains uniquely best against A and C, so the item is not broken — but the per-letter claim did change, not merely shorten.
style.quote_before: The decision to build a laddered bond portfolio should be weighed against buying shares in a fixed-income mutual fund, especially if the portfolio consists of a limited number of corporate bonds.
style.quote_after: it diversifies default risk less well than a fixed-income mutual fund.

style.detail: A figure inside what is presented as a direct curriculum quotation was silently altered in the C rationale: before "These ETFs have a designated year of maturity and credit risk profile — for instance, 2024 investment-grade corporate bonds", after "These ETFs have a designated year of maturity and credit risk profile, for instance 2029 investment-grade corporate bonds". No reasoning depends on the year and the change does harmonize the rationale with the option's own "2029" example, so nothing is broken; but the rewrite was not licensed to change numbers in the rationale, and the adjacent "Roughly equal positions in a series of such funds, say 2022 through 2029" was left untouched, so the edit was deliberate rather than mechanical.
style.quote_before: for instance, 2024 investment-grade corporate bonds
style.quote_after: for instance 2029 investment-grade corporate bonds

style.detail: The key's proposition was replaced with its consequence, and the old proposition was moved into the stem. Before, C asserted the shared data dependence itself: "Both rely on reported returns of alternatives, which are subject to STALE PRICING and APPRAISAL SMOOTHING." After, C asserts the resulting bias: "Understated volatility in both, biasing toward overallocation." The stem now supplies the old C as a given — before: "Weakness common to BOTH the asset-class and risk-factor approaches when applied to alternatives most likely:" / after: "Smoothed and stale reported returns on alternative investments affect the asset-class approach and the risk-factor approach to allocation most likely as:" So the tested content shifts from recognizing that both approaches inherit the smoothed-returns problem to knowing the direction of the bias. NOT fatal: the new C is correct (it is stated verbatim in the before rationale, "both approaches understate true volatility and correlations, biasing efficient frontiers toward overallocation to alternatives"), A and B remain false (A reverses direction, B is refuted because factor decomposition is estimated from the same return series), the key stays in C and the item is unambiguous and answerable. Flagged only because the item was already self-contained (no exhibit, no citation), and the spec says "Do not reframe an item that is already self-contained"; the shortening could have been done as a restatement of the original claim instead. Secondary: option B, "Distortion of the asset-class approach only.", is not grammatically parallel with A and C, which are both "<direction> volatility in both, biasing toward <direction>".
style.quote_before: Both rely on reported returns of alternatives, which are subject to STALE PRICING and APPRAISAL SMOOTHING.
style.quote_after: Understated volatility in both, biasing toward overallocation.

style.detail: The rewritten stem asks for a tax character ("the tax character of hedge fund returns is most likely:"), and A and C both answer with one ("short-term gains taxed at ordinary rates." / "long-term gains taxed at favorable rates."). B instead answers with a materiality judgment about the suitability assessment, so the three options are no longer the same kind of thing (house style rule 7). The claim itself is preserved from "before" and B is still false, so the key is unaffected; it merely makes B discardable on shape rather than on knowledge. A parallel re-voicing in the same register as A and C (e.g. a third candidate tax character) would fix it.
style.quote_before: B: "Tax considerations are irrelevant to hedge fund suitability for private clients." (stem: "High-net-worth taxable investor's suitability considerations for hedge funds most likely:")
style.quote_after: stem: "For a high-net-worth taxable investor, the tax character of hedge fund returns is most likely:" / B: "immaterial to the suitability assessment."

style.detail: The rewrite broadened the stem's asset-class scope from private equity to closed-end funds generally, while two of the three options (B, C) still speak specifically of "private equity" and distractor A contrasts hedge funds with private equity. The key (B) is still correct and still clearly best, and the item remains answerable, so this is not fatal; but the new scope makes A a free reject on a technicality the item does not intend to test -- hedge funds are not closed-end funds, so a learner can discard A from the stem's wording alone without knowing anything about vintage-year dispersion. Under the old stem ("in private equity") A was a live, substantive distractor about where the effect lives. Narrowing the stem back to private equity, or re-voicing A as "an effect of manager selection rather than of inception timing," would restore the three-way discrimination.
style.quote_before: Vintage-year effects in private equity most likely:
style.quote_after: Vintage-year effects in closed-end fund returns are best described as:

style.detail: Distractor B's rewritten rationale ends in a garbled, ungrammatical clause. The old rationale closed cleanly on the point that stress brings 'wider discounts and paused distributions, not improved access'; the rewrite tries to rebut the original distractor's 'distressed buyers compete to purchase LP interests' and produces 'rather than competing access open', which is not a sentence. The reasoning is still recoverable and the item itself is correctly keyed (C, 'worse'), so this is cosmetic, not fatal.
style.quote_before: Reverses reality; liquidity deeply contracts in stress, with wider discounts and paused distributions, not improved access.
style.quote_after: Buyers in the secondary market gain bargaining power over distressed sellers rather than competing access open.

style.detail: The correct option's rationale drops the named fraud exemplar that anchored the claim about why ODD carries veto authority. Nothing is made wrong by this and the key (B) is still the only correct option, but the rationale is less concrete than the one it replaced and the spec asks rationales to get longer, not to shed specifics.

style.quote_after: Operational failures are a leading cause of hedge fund fraud losses, so ODD often carries veto authority in institutional programs.

style.detail: Option A was shortened so that its justification clause ('to simplify tracking and reporting') is gone, but rationale A was rewritten to add a rebuttal of exactly that dropped clause. The rationale now answers a claim the learner can no longer see in the option it is explaining. The key (B) is unaffected and A is still false for the reason given in the first half of the rationale.
style.quote_before: Concentrate all commitments in a single vintage year to simplify tracking and reporting. / rationale: Single-vintage concentration creates cyclical timing risk; the goal is deploying across vintages to smooth exposure.

style.detail: The correct option's rationale replaces the named strategy-specific benchmark with a generic paraphrase, so the learner no longer gets the actual index family the curriculum points at. The reasoning and the 'cash plus 400 bps' absolute-benchmark example survive, and the key (C) remains correct and uniquely so, so this is a specificity loss in the explanation only.

style.quote_after: Strategy-specific benchmarks are preferred, such as an equity market-neutral index for a market-neutral fund, and peer groups with a similar strategy and risk profile are also useful.

style.detail: Rationale C's closing sentence changed what it asserts about where credit/spread strategies are handled. "before" says the reading covers the first three components, adds currency in a later section, and that credit/spread work is outside this reading: "The reading focuses on actively managing the first three components (yield curve strategies) and adds currency in Section 4; credit/spread strategies come later." "after" drops the section citation (correctly, per rule 9) but re-assigns the topic: "currency is added separately, and credit or spread strategies are treated with the fourth." The before sentence places credit/spread strategies elsewhere in the curriculum; the after sentence tells the learner they are treated here, alongside the fourth component, and "the fourth" has no antecedent in the sentence (the fourth component? the fourth section?). The key (C) is still correct and still clearly the best of the three, A and B remain false, and every letter carries its prior claim, so the item is not broken — but this sentence now says something the before rationale did not, and the simplest repair is to restore "credit and spread strategies are covered later" without the section number.
style.quote_before: The reading focuses on actively managing the first three components (yield curve strategies) and adds currency in Section 4; credit/spread strategies come later.
style.quote_after: currency is added separately, and credit or spread strategies are treated with the fourth

style.detail: Distractor A was narrowed from "no change in slope" to "no change in yields at all". These are not the same claim: the original admitted a parallel shift (yields move, slope does not), the rewrite admits only a frozen curve. Both remain false against the stem and the rewritten rationale ("Yields unchanged at both ends is a static view, not a steepening at all") describes the option as it now reads, so the key (B) is untouched and nothing is double-keyed. Flagged only because the letter no longer carries the claim it carried before; the shortening also drops the one case the original distractor was testing, namely that a parallel shift is not a steepener.
style.quote_before: A scenario with no slope change.
style.quote_after: Short- and long-term yields unchanged.

style.detail: The rewrite de-Unicoded the key rate duration formula in rationale B and in doing so changed the operator from a discrete change to a derivative. 'Before' carries the curriculum's Equation 10 as KeyRateDur_k = -(1/PV) x (DeltaPV / Delta r_k) with the proper minus sign, multiplication sign and Sigma for the summation; 'after' writes dPV / dr_k with an ASCII hyphen, a lowercase letter x for the multiplication sign, and spells the summation out as 'sum of KeyRateDur_k = EffDur'.
